title: Auditory Perception and Cognitive Performance
authors: Angélique A. Scharine et al., Undated
review_question: How do auditory perception and its underlying psychoacoustic relationships influence cognitive performance and human interaction with the acoustic environment?
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Not explicitly specified; the review synthesizes findings from a broad range of psychoacoustic and auditory perception research.

findings.quote: The minimum level of stimulation required to evoke a physiologic response from the auditory system is called the threshold of hearing or detection threshold and depends on the frequency, duration, and spectral complexity of the stimulus.

The audibility of low frequency stimuli improves with increasing frequency at an average rate of about 12 dB/octave and typically decreases with age, from 20 to 70 years of age, by 10 dB or less for frequencies below 500 Hz.

findings.consequent: audibility of high frequency stimuli (above 8,000 Hz)
findings.quote: The typical changes in the threshold of hearing with age, from 20 to 70 years of age, at frequencies above 8,000 Hz, exceed 60 dB in normally hearing population.
the auditory system is especially sensitive to sound energy in the 1.5 to 6 kHz range with the most sensitive region being in the 3.0 to 4.0 kHz range (Moore, 1997).
The binaural thresholds of hearing shown in Figure 11-1 and Table 11-1 are approximately 2 dB lower than the corresponding monaural thresholds if both ears have similar sensitivity.

findings.antecedent: occluding ear canal by an earphone
findings.consequent: amplification of low frequency physiologic noise (e.g., blood flow noise) and elevation of MAP threshold
findings.quote: occluding the ear canal by an earphone was reported to cause an amplification of low frequency physiologic noise (e.g., blood flow noise) by the closed cavity of the ear canal and elevation of MAP threshold at low frequencies.

findings.antecedent: background noise level (30 to 70 dB SPL range)
findings.quote: the threshold of discomfort is almost independent of background noise level (in 30 to 70 dB SPL range) and exceeds 80 dB SPL.

The typical difference between the most comfortable listening level and threshold of discomfort is about 15 dB for pure tones and speech (Dirks and Kamm, 1976) and about 25 dB for noises (Sammeth, Birman and Hecox, 1989).

findings.antecedent: sound intensity (infrasound below 20 Hz, exceeding 115 dB)
findings.consequent: disorientation, pain, feeling of pressure on the chest
findings.quote: such tones having sufficiently high sound intensity levels are not heard but immediately felt causing disorientation, pain, and feeling of pressure on the chest.
hearing sensitivity, especially in the high frequency region, declines with age (Galton, 1883; Robinson and Dadson, 1957), exposure to noise, and use of ototoxic drugs...
The threshold of hearing is not the same for all populations and depends on both gender and ethnicity.
At the low levels of stimulation, the actual differential thresholds are larger than predicted by Weber's Law due to the presence of internal noise.

findings.antecedent: single-event stimulus change (step without interstimulus pause)
findings.quote: If the single-event stimulus change has the form of a step without any interstimulus pause, the differential threshold is generally smaller than the modulation detection thresholds.

The tendency of the auditory system to smooth out (ignore) small frequently repeated changes in an auditory stimulus can be, among others, observed in the decrease of audibility of modulation with increasing modulation rate.

findings.antecedent: sound intensity level (greater than 20 dB above threshold)
findings.quote: The DL for sound intensity is typically about 0.5 to 1.0 dB within a wide range of intensities (greater than 20 dB above the threshold) and across many types of stimuli.

The intensity DL (in dB) is independent of stimulus duration for durations exceeding 200 millisecond (ms) and increases at a rate of about 3 dB per halving the duration for durations shorter than 200 ms.
at low frequencies (below 500 Hz) the DL for frequency (in Hz) is relatively independent of frequency and increases logarithmically with frequency at mid and high frequencies.
the frequency DL decreases with increasing duration of short auditory stimuli and becomes independent of duration for stimuli exceeding 100 to 200 ms.
Note also a very profound effect of training on frequency discrimination and recognition.
the duration DL of uniform (steady-state) sounds follows Weber's Law with a Weber fraction of around 0.1 to 0.2 for time durations greater than about 20 ms.
Sounds with ramped down temporal envelopes are perceived as shorter, and sounds with ramped up temporal envelopes are perceived as longer than those with a uniform envelope.
It also has been reported that presentation of sound-distracter affects visual time-order perception.
Auditory adaptation, or loudness adaptation, is a gradual decrease in hearing sensitivity during sustained, fixed-level, auditory stimulation.

findings.antecedent: excessive stimulation (continuous noise > 85 dB SPL, impulse noise > 140 dB SPL)
findings.quote: Exposure to recurring or extreme acoustic trauma can result in permanent hearing loss.

findings.antecedent: presence of two or more sounds (concurrent or in close succession)
findings.quote: The concurrent, or in close succession, presence of two or more sounds causes the audibility of the individual sounds to be adversely affected by the presence of other sounds.

findings.antecedent: masker intensity (in frequency region of target sound)
findings.quote: When the masker contains sufficient energy in the frequency region of the target sound, the masked threshold increases about 10 dB for every 10 dB increase in masker.

findings.antecedent: simultaneous presence of signal energy in several critical bands
findings.quote: simultaneous presence of signal energy in several critical bands aids signal detection.

findings.antecedent: time difference between masker offset and target onset
findings.quote: Masking decreases as the intensity of the masker decreases, the separation between the sounds increases, and the time difference between the two offsets increases.

findings.antecedent: similarity between masker and target sound, variability (uncertainty) of masker
findings.quote: Two main causes of informational masking are similarity between the masker and the target sound and the variability (uncertainty) of the masker.
the effectiveness of informational masking increases with age even in people with otologically normal hearing.

findings.antecedent: sound components (within a narrow frequency band smaller than a single critical band)
findings.quote: if the sound components are located within a narrow frequency band smaller than a single critical band, the total loudness of sound is proportional to the total sound energy contained within the band.

findings.antecedent: sound components (separated further apart than a critical band)
findings.quote: If the sound components are separated further apart than a critical band, the sound loudness is the sum of the loudnesses of the individual components.

findings.antecedent: sound duration (shorter than critical duration, ~200-300 ms)
findings.quote: For sounds shorter than critical duration, the loudness of sound increases with sound duration and this relationship can be described as: SIL x T = constant loudness.

findings.antecedent: listener listening to sound at Most Comfortable Loudness (MCL)
findings.quote: listening to sound at the MCL results in the best and most consistent human performance.

findings.antecedent: listening at levels other than MCL
findings.quote: Listening at levels other than the MCL also demands increased attention resources and causes the listener to become fatigued more rapidly.

findings.antecedent: background noise level (up to 40 dB SPL)
findings.quote: noise levels up to 40 dB SPL have a negligible effect on the MCL for speech.

findings.antecedent: increase in noise levels (above 40 dB SPL)
findings.quote: the MCL increases about 7 dB per 10 dB of increase in noise levels, up to about 100 dB SPL.

findings.consequent: perceived sound image clarity, listener fatigue
findings.quote: it also makes the perceived sound image less clear due to nonlinear distortions generated in the middle ear and is more tiring.
for middle frequencies (1 to 2 kHz in Stevens' and 2.5 kHz in Gullick's case), the pitch of a pure tone is independent of the stimulus intensity.
for tones of higher frequencies, increased sound intensity produces an increase in pitch. Conversely, for tones of lower frequencies, increased sound intensity produces a decrease in pitch.
listeners perceived the rising sound intensity as an upward shift in pitch.

findings.antecedent: frequency components (separated by more than one critical band)
findings.consequent: audibility of absolute or relative phase difference
findings.quote: people are sensitive to neither absolute nor relative phase difference between various components of the periodic stimulus if the components are separated in their frequencies by more than one critical band.

findings.antecedent: frequency components (fall into same critical band, small frequency difference)
findings.consequent: audibility of phase relationship changes, pitch value, pitch clarity
findings.quote: if two frequency components, e.g., harmonics, fall into the same critical band and their difference in frequency is rather small, the changes in their phase relationship are audible and affect both pitch value and pitch clarity.
Two physical factors are commonly mentioned as physical correlates of timbre: the spectral envelope and the temporal envelope of the sound.
timbre is the perceptual property of sound that reflects unique properties of the sound and its sound source.

findings.consequent: listener annoyance, listening comfort, long-term performance
findings.quote: If speech quality is relatively low, it may cause listener's annoyance and affect listening comfort and long-term performance of the listener.

findings.antecedent: emotional state, expectations, activity of a person
findings.consequent: perceived duration (of long lasting acoustic events)
findings.quote: perceived duration is primarily dependent on emotional state, expectations, and activity of a person and is very difficult to generalize.
pleasant events appear to last shorter (time contraction) and unpleasant events longer (time dilation) than their actual physical durations.

In the case of very short acoustic events, humans have a general tendency to overestimate sound duration, and the amount of overestimation seems to be inversely proportional to the actual duration of the sound.

findings.consequent: perceived duration (differs greatly from physical duration)
findings.quote: One important condition where perceived duration differs greatly from the physical duration is perception of short silent intervals.
short pauses seem to last as much as 2 to 4 times longer than short sound bursts of the same duration.
The error in sensory judgment resulting from sequential presentation of stimuli is referred to as the time error (TE) or sequential error.

findings.antecedent: short time gaps (due to forward masking)
findings.quote: In the case of short time gaps when the TE is primarily a result of a forward masking, the TE is positive (+TE).

findings.antecedent: long time gaps (due to decaying memory trace)
findings.quote: In the case of long time gaps, when the time error is due to decaying memory trace of the first stimulus, the TE is negative (-TE).
if the speech sounds are unfamiliar to the listener... the speech looses its special character caused by coupling between speech perception and speech production of the listener.

findings.consequent: talker's voice (Lombard effect: vowel duration, intensity, fundamental frequency, spectral envelope)
findings.quote: The Lombard effect (Lombard, 1911) is a phenomenon in which a talker alters his or her voice in noisy environments. Generally, there is an increase in vowel duration and voice intensity.
signal processing techniques that replicate the Lombard effect improve the intelligibility of speech in a noise environment.
Good understanding of speech requires high SNRs in the order of 15 to 30 dB. Smaller SNRs lead to reduced speech intelligibility scores.
the absolute level of the noise has a minimal effect on speech understanding as long as the noise levels are below 85 dB SPL.

findings.antecedent: random, unpredictable noise or noise with similar temporal/spectral characteristics to speech
findings.consequent: informational masking (in addition to energetic masking)
findings.quote: random, unpredictable noise, or noise where the temporal and spectral characteristics are similar to that of speech, can add informational masking to the energetic masking.
An acoustic environment can also add reverberation to the speech signal. Reverberation consists of multiple reflections of the sound that mask the direct sound.

findings.antecedent: spatial separation (of talker and noise sources)
findings.quote: If the two signals are separated in space, binaural cues can be used to separate the two locations, and the listener can selectively attend to the target speech signal.
Speech intelligibility performance generally improves as the material becomes more complex and contains more contextual information and higher degree of redundancy.
A trained talker such as radio announcer who speaks clearly will be more intelligible than a talker using normal conversational speech.
a female voice is generally more intelligible than a male voice.
Many reports have shown an advantage of binaural listening for speech recognition.

findings.antecedent: binaural listening (better ear advantage, spatial localization cues)
findings.consequent: speech information separation from noise, attention to speech location
findings.quote: binaural listening allows the listener to utilize the better ear advantage... the listener can use spatial localization cues... to separate the speech information from the noise and can attend to the spatial location of the speech.

findings.antecedent: auditory spatial perception (directions, distances, ambience, spaciousness)
findings.consequent: navigation through space, feeling of spaciousness
findings.quote: This perception encompasses sensations (perceptions) of directions in horizontal and vertical plane, recognition of auditory distance and auditory depth, and sensation (perception) of ambience (perceived size of space) that together allow us to navigate through the space and feel its spaciousness.

findings.consequent: binaural threshold of hearing, binaural loudness
findings.quote: Diotic presentation of a stimulus results in the lower binaural threshold of hearing and the higher binaural loudness than the respective monaural (single ear) responses.
the ear disparity may lead to difficulties in pitch perception, called binaural displacusis.

findings.antecedent: target sound or noise (phase reversed 180° in one ear)
findings.quote: when the phase of either the target sound or noise is reversed 180° in phase in one of the ears, the audibility of the target sounds markedly improves.
If the same sound is received by both ears, the sound source is perceived as located in the median plane of the listener.

findings.antecedent: sound source (side of head, off median plane)
findings.quote: If the sounds differ in their time of arrival and/or intensity, the sound source is perceived as being located at a certain azimuth angle to the left or to the right of the median plane but not at the median plane.

findings.antecedent: head size (d) and sound wavelength (λ) (d >> λ)
findings.quote: The larger the difference between d and λ (d >> λ), the stronger the baffling effect.
a fast sound source movement makes it more difficult to identify the momentary position of sound source.

findings.antecedent: reflected sounds (arriving shortly after original sound)
findings.consequent: listener awareness of reflected sound, sound localization accuracy
findings.quote: Most of the time, the listener is unaware of this reflected sound, and to some extent continues to be able to localize the sound accurately in spite of the presence of reflected sounds.

findings.antecedent: second sound (delayed up to 30-40 ms, intensity not exceeding first sound by >10 dB)
findings.quote: the perception of the second of two successively received similar sounds is suppressed if the second sound is delayed up to about 30 to 40 ms, and its intensity does not exceed the intensity of the first sound by more than 10 dB.

findings.antecedent: sound source (familiarity with original sound, surrounding space)
findings.consequent: sound localization ability (vertical plane, front-back axis)
findings.quote: sound localization ability, especially in the vertical plane and along the front-back axis, improves with experience and familiarization with both the stimuli and environment.
Small movements of the head from the left to the right will quickly clarify whether the sound is in the front or rear hemisphere. Vertical movements give salient elevation information.
For familiar sounds, one can compare the loudness of the perceived sound with the knowledge about the natural loudness and intensity of its source.
the distance to an unfamiliar sound source (or a sound source that may have various sound loudnesses at the source) is difficult to estimate using the loudness cue.
According to the inverse square law of sound propagation in open space, sound intensity decreases by 6 dB per doubling of the distance from the sound source.

In enclosed spaces, wall reflections reduce this intensity drop associated with the distance from the sound source and at some critical distance, which is a function of the sound source distance from the listener and the reflecting walls, obviate the cue altogether.

findings.consequent: low frequency energy (relative to high frequency)
findings.quote: Consequently, distant sounds will have relatively more low frequency energy than the same sounds radiated from proximal (nearby) sound sources and result in different sound timbre.

findings.consequent: distance perception (in closed spaces or echo situations)
findings.quote: The third cue, reverberance or liveness, is a major cue for distance perception in closed spaces or in situations that produce an echo.

findings.consequent: sound clarity, sound source location certainty
findings.quote: If the distance is large, the sound becomes less clear and its sound source location less certain.
when the listener moves (translates) the head, the change in the azimuth toward the sound source is distance dependent. This cue is called the motion parallax cue.

findings.antecedent: perceived auditory distance (to talker in audio channel, different from 1-1.5 m)
findings.quote: If the perceived auditory distance to another talker in an audio channel is quite different from 1 to 1.5 m, such voice communication will distract the operator, increase the workload, and increase the overall level of anxiety.

findings.consequent: transmission of acoustic energy into middle ear
findings.quote: Most conductive hearing losses within the outer ear partially or completely block the transmission of acoustic energy into the middle ear and they are treatable.

findings.antecedent: resonance of pinna and outer ear canal (2 to 7 kHz)
findings.consequent: listener's ability to localize and perceive acoustic space
findings.quote: The resonance of the pinna and the outer ear canal is between 2 to 7 kHz, which enhances the ability of the listener to localize and perceive their acoustic space.
Sensorineural hearing loss is characterized by irreversible damage that distorts auditory perception.

findings.antecedent: excessive exposure to sounds (2000 to 6000 Hz)
findings.quote: Excessive exposure to sounds energy in the frequency range from 2000 to 6000 Hz is most likely to cause permanent changes in hearing.

Given that background noise is generally low-frequency, this type of noise can exacerbate a high-frequency hearing loss since it can mask the portion of the signal that the listener is able to hear in quiet.

synthesis_conclusions: Auditory perception is a complex, multi-dimensional process influenced by physical stimulus characteristics (intensity, frequency, duration, spectral/temporal envelopes), environmental context (noise, reverberation, spatial configuration), and individual listener factors (age, gender, training, hearing status).

Basic auditory sensations (loudness, pitch, perceived duration) form the foundation for higher-level cognitive processes like recognition and identification, which are crucial for effective communication and interaction with the acoustic environment.
Auditory thresholds (hearing, discomfort, pain) vary significantly with frequency, duration, and individual differences, highlighting the need for context-specific assessment and design.

Masking (energetic and informational) and temporal processing limitations (e.g., precedence effect, time error) significantly impact audibility, speech intelligibility, and sound localization, especially in complex or noisy environments.

Spatial auditory perception relies on a combination of binaural (ILD, ITD) and monaural (HRTF, pinna reflections) cues, which are enhanced by head movements and listener familiarity with the environment.

Speech communication effectiveness is highly dependent on SNR, reverberation, talker characteristics (e.g., Lombard effect, gender), listener characteristics (hearing loss, training), and the linguistic context of the message.
Sound quality, encompassing aesthetic and utilitarian aspects, is crucial for listener satisfaction and long-term performance, even beyond basic intelligibility.
evidence_gaps: Environmental sound research is still in its beginning stages, with few quantitative studies reporting thresholds of hearing for various environmental and man-made sounds.
There is a lack of strict standards for calculating bilateral Pure Tone Average (PTA) for binaural hearing loss.

Current speech intelligibility indexes (AI, STI) do not fully account for the spatial arrangement of sound sources in the operational environment or the full degree of speech communication (beyond recognition of phonemes/syllables).
The physiological mechanism responsible for auditory adaptation is still not clear.
The physiologic basis of backward masking is still largely unknown.

moderators.effect: Age influences audibility of low and high frequency stimuli, with high frequency hearing declining significantly with age. Older individuals also show increased susceptibility to informational masking.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Women generally have better hearing than men, but with aging, women have poorer capacity to hear lower frequencies, while men's thresholds worsen at higher frequencies.

moderators.effect: Gender influences hearing thresholds and patterns of age-related hearing loss, with women generally having better hearing than men, especially at higher frequencies.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Women of all ages have better hearing than men above 2000 Hz, but with aging, women have poorer capacity to hear lower frequencies than men.

moderators.effect: Background noise level affects the Most Comfortable Loudness (MCL) for speech, with negligible effect up to 40 dB SPL, but increasing MCL by ~7 dB for every 10 dB increase in noise above this level.

Stimulus duration affects intensity DL (increasing for durations shorter than 200 ms) and frequency DL (decreasing with increasing duration for short stimuli). It also affects perceived duration, with short sounds overestimated and short pauses perceived as longer.
These factors are the main causes of informational masking, with higher similarity and uncertainty leading to greater masking effects.

limitations: The chapter acknowledges that many reported threshold values are based on pure tones and may not directly apply to complex natural sounds like speech or environmental sounds.
It notes that speech intelligibility measures are limited by the representativeness of speech material and talker characteristics to real-world operational environments.
The chapter highlights that current objective speech intelligibility indexes (AI, STI) do not fully account for temporal distortions, non-linear effects, or spatial arrangement of sound sources.
It states that the mel and bark scales for pitch are developed for pure tones and do not directly apply to speech and music.
The review acknowledges that auditory distance estimation is relatively poor, especially for absolute judgments, and that people tend to underestimate distance exponentially.

paper_metadata.title: Emotion and perception: the role of affective information.
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Emotion and perception: the role of affective information
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract:
AbstractVisual perception and emotion are traditionally considered separate domains of study. In this article, however, we review research showing them to be less separable than usually assumed. In fact, emotions routinely affect how and what we see. Fear, for example, can affect low‐level visual processes, sad moods can alter susceptibility to visual illusions, and goal‐directed desires can change the apparent size of goal‐relevant objects. In addition, the layout of the physical environment, including the apparent steepness of a hill and the distance to the ground from a balcony can both be affected by emotional states. We propose that emotions provide embodied information about the costs and benefits of anticipated action, information that can be used automatically and immediately, circumventing the need for cogitating on the possible consequences of potential actions. Emotions thus provide a strong motivating influence on how the environment is perceived. WIREs Cogni Sci 2011 2 676–685 DOI: 10.1002/wcs.147This article is categorized under:

Psychology > Emotion and Motivation

environmental_features: environmental sounds (e.g., nature sounds, traffic noise)
various types of noise (e.g., white noise, pink noise, speech-shaped noise, office noise)
stimulus_description.duration_exposure: variable, ranging from milliseconds (for discrete stimuli) to continuous exposure over minutes or hours (for background soundscapes)
control_conditions: different types of auditory stimuli (e.g., comparing speech to music, or different noise types)

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Auditory stimuli, particularly irrelevant speech or noise, can increase extraneous cognitive load, thereby reducing available resources for primary task performance.
Cognitive performance depends on the allocation of limited attentional resources, which can be diverted or depleted by distracting auditory stimuli.
Auditory stimuli can influence physiological and psychological arousal levels, which in turn can modulate cognitive performance according to the Yerkes-Dodson law.
Changes in auditory stimulation, particularly the presence of varying irrelevant sounds, can disrupt serial recall and other cognitive tasks, even when attention is directed elsewhere.

mechanism_chain.description: The paper reviews various causal pathways through which auditory stimuli influence cognitive performance, often involving attentional processes, cognitive load, and emotional/arousal states.

steps.to_construct: Reduced cognitive performance (e.g., impaired memory, slower reaction times, increased errors)

steps.from_construct: Auditory stimulus (e.g., loud noise, unpleasant sounds)

steps.to_construct: Changes in attentional focus and resource allocation

steps.from_construct: Changes in attentional focus and resource allocation
steps.to_construct: Modulated cognitive performance (e.g., impaired complex tasks, enhanced simple tasks)

instruments_used.name: N-back task
instruments_used.description: A continuous performance task requiring participants to indicate if the current stimulus matches one presented 'n' steps earlier.

instruments_used.name: Stroop task
instruments_used.description: A task measuring reaction time and accuracy when naming the color of a word, especially when the word itself is a different color name.

instruments_used.name: Serial recall tasks
instruments_used.description: Tasks requiring participants to recall a sequence of items (e.g., digits, letters) in the order they were presented.

instruments_used.name: Reaction time tasks
instruments_used.description: Measures the time taken to respond to a stimulus.

instruments_used.name: Electroencephalography (EEG)
instruments_used.description: Measures electrical activity in the brain, often used to identify specific brain responses to auditory stimuli (e.g., P300, N1, MMN).

instruments_used.name: Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI)
instruments_used.construct: brain activity, neural correlates of cognition
instruments_used.description: Measures changes in blood flow to detect areas of brain activity during auditory perception and cognitive tasks.

instruments_used.name: Heart Rate Variability (HRV)
instruments_used.description: Measures the variation in the time interval between heartbeats, used as an indicator of autonomic nervous system activity.

instruments_used.name: Subjective ratings (e.g., annoyance, perceived effort, mood scales)
instruments_used.description: Self-report questionnaires assessing participants' subjective experience of auditory stimuli or task demands.
